prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and thereby changing the understanding of exporting, reallocation and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Melitz (2003) moved trade theory from representative industries to heterogeneous firms. Selection into exporting, reallocation across firms and a new channel for gains from trade followed from that move. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) extended it to the exporting-versus-FDI choice. The framework is now the standard foundation for trade analysis, and it spread into firm-level empirics, productivity and growth, and policy evaluation. It has more than two decades of confirmation. Trade has not been recognised since 2008. Every colleague who proposed laureates for this ballot named the same pair, Melitz and Helpman, so the attribution is unusually clean. I moved this ballot to first place because the attribution problem on B021 is more serious than I weighed in my opening. Under a three-name cap any B021 trio leaves out major contributors, and I do not think I can defend a citation that cuts so deep. The importance of B021 is not in doubt.
statement.case_against: Credit for the firm-heterogeneity agenda is spread more widely than two names suggest. Bernard and Jensen on exporter premia, Eaton and Kortum on quantitative trade, and Redding on later quantitative and spatial work all have claims, and the ballot omits some of them. Some welfare-gains results in this literature are sensitive to functional-form and parametric assumptions. Helpman also appears on B007, so the Committee would be choosing which body of his work to honour. Finally, I am setting aside B021, which I ranked first, partly on attribution grounds. That makes the choice a judgment about which problem is more tractable, not about which field matters more.

responses.point: Andersson ranks Grossman and Helpman (B007) first. He cites a clean two-person attribution, the very high maturity of the 1990s political-economy-of-protection work, and a framework that links trade to political economy. He also notes that empirical support for the lobbying model's precise predictions is mixed.
responses.response: I agree the attribution on B007 is clean, and the pair's endogenous-growth and trade work adds to their standing. But Helpman is the shared name, so the two ballots compete for the same laureate. On common criteria I judge firm heterogeneity to have the broader and better-confirmed reach. It changed theory, firm-level microdata work, quantitative policy evaluation and the productivity literature. By Andersson's own account the lobbying model's empirical record is mixed. I would not close the door on a Grossman–Helpman recognition later, but I would not put it ahead of Melitz–Helpman now.

responses.point: Friberg ranks Kiyotaki and Moore (B043) first. He argues the collateral-constraint mechanism is cleanly theirs, has three decades of confirmation, became the template for financial-friction macroeconomics after 2008, and is not itself covered by the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution. I ranked B043 third and keep it as an alternative. My reservation is thematic. The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, with Bernanke's accelerator, covers adjacent ground, so the marginal novelty of another financial-friction award is lower than for a field that has been unrecognised since 2008. Direct empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification is also still debated. This is a difference of priority, not a doubt about Kiyotaki–Moore's merit. If the Committee prefers a macro-finance award, I would support the two-person version.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the Berry–Levinsohn–Pakes demand-estimation and dynamic-industry framework (B029) first. He stresses its standard use in merger and antitrust analysis, trade and environmental policy, and the three decades of validation. He keeps the three-name cap on the BLP core and treats Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin as adjacent.
responses.response: I agree that B029 is prize-level and that the BLP trio is the cleanest cut, which is why I ranked it fourth. Two things keep it below B012 for me. The ballot lists seven names, so any three-name cut invites a dispute over Bresnahan's claim on the demand side. The prize would also be read mainly as a methods prize, and I weigh that differently from a change in how economists understand a core economic phenomenon such as the gains from trade. These are close judgments, and Krusell's practical case for B029 is strong.

responses.point: Dreber ranks population-data work on mobility (B014) first. She argues it is credible by design, with very large samples, quasi-experimental designs and transparent data, and that it has shaped both research and policy.
responses.response: I share her view of the design quality and the policy influence, but I rank it seventh. Most of the core results date from 2014 to 2022. The causal reading of neighbourhood effects is still under scrutiny, and credit is spread across a large collaborative team, so the limit of three names forces arbitrary exclusions. I would give it more weight if replication and long-run follow-up settle the place-effect estimates. The mobility literature that Solon, Björklund–Jäntti and Corak established earlier also complicates a claim to novelty.

uncertainties: Whether adding Redding as a third laureate would better reflect the quantitative follow-on literature, or only dilute a clean pair.
How the Committee would weigh credit for Bernard–Jensen and Eaton–Kortum, who are outside this ballot but made parallel empirical and quantitative contributions.
Whether Helpman's recognition is better framed through B012 or B007, since only one prize can name him.
Whether my move away from B021 reflects its attribution problem or an excess of caution, and whether a differently framed B021 citation could repair it.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent with Melitz or Helpman from the supplied profile. As chair I disclose collegial ties: I have co-authored with committee members Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, Per Krusell is a frequent co-author, and I am an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. None of them is a credited name on B012. I also gave the 2018 presentation speech and my own work is cited in the 2018 background, which does not bear on this ballot.
